newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian farmers reject Iran trade ban calls.
newsitem.headline: Australian farmers reject Iran trade ban calls.

text.p: Australian wheat farmers urged the government on Sunday to reject calls to ban trade with Iran after a German court found Tehran ordered the murders of four Kurdish activists in Berlin in 1992.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer is reviewing relations with Iran after the court ruling and on Friday recalled ambassador Stuart Hume from Tehran.
Queensland Graingrowers Association president Ian MacFarlane said farmers could not afford a trade ban on the country's major wheat market.
"Iran is a market worth up to A$500 million (US$390 million) a year to us, and it's one which we don't want endangered by politicking and by trade sanctions," he said in a statement.
The Australian Wheat Board has also warned against trade retaliation.

Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer said any further Australian retaliation would not hit already-agreed sales. Iran has contracted to buy about 2.8 million tonnes of Australian wheat, some of which has already been delivered.
Australia's Labor opposition has urged an immediate trade ban and the cancellation of a A$950 million (US$750 million) line of credit.

But two-way trade is heavily in Australia's favour -- A$650 million in Australian exports and A$28 million in imports from Iran in calendar 1996. Apart from wheat, Australia's main exports to Iran are wool, sugar, vegetable oils and meat.
Australia does not release details of its total wheat exports but in fiscal 1995-96 they were worth $3.75 billion.
India is the country's second largest wheat market with contracts totalling 2.35 million tonnes signed this year.
Western nations have taken a series of retaliatory measures against Iran after the German court ruling last week.

The court said Iran's political leadership ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992. It avoided names but said the assassination was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, religious leader, intelligence minister and head of foreign policy.
Downer said Australia would consider further responses to the court decision after studying the verdict.
